title: KPT step 1: double consonants
summary: Learn why Finnish words use strong and weak grades, then practise the three most visible KPT changes: kk → k, pp → p, and tt → t.
objectives: Understand strong and weak grade in plain English.
Produce a supplied weak form without learning another KPT family.

sections.title: Why one word can have two grades
paragraphs: Many Finnish words use two closely related versions of the same stem. One uses the strong grade and the other uses the weak grade. When an ending is added, Finnish grammar can select a different grade while the word keeps the same basic meaning.
Strong and weak are simply names for consonant patterns. They do not mean that one form is better, more forceful, or more correct than the other.
We begin with double consonants because their change is especially easy to see. Other KPT families have different strong–weak pairs, which later lessons introduce separately.
keyPoints: begin with the clearest visible change

sections.title: One letter remains
paragraphs: A double consonant has two identical consonant letters. In the double-consonant family taught here, the strong grade has the pair and the weak grade has one letter.
This is one KPT family, not a definition of every strong and weak grade in Finnish.

sections.title: Keep the ending separate
paragraphs: First notice or make the consonant change. Then read the ending already shown in the complete form.
This lesson does not ask you to predict single-consonant or cluster changes.

steps: Pankki and pankin are forms of the same word; the basic meaning “bank” remains.
Adding the genitive ending -n selects the weak grade here: the strong kk becomes weak k.
The ending -n is separate from the consonant change: pankki → panki- → pankin.
The two p letters become one: pp → p.
The complete supplied form is kaupan.
The two t letters become one: tt → t.
The complete supplied form is maton.

commonMistakes: Do not apply a single-consonant rule in this lesson.
The final ending is not part of the KPT change.

practiceExercises.prompt: What changes in pankki (“bank”) → pankin (“of the bank”)?
practiceExercises.explanation: The double kk becomes one k.

optionFeedback.kk → k: Correct. The double kk becomes one k.
optionFeedback.k → ∅: “k → ∅” does not show the required pattern. The double kk becomes one k.
optionFeedback.nk → ng: “nk → ng” does not show the required pattern. The double kk becomes one k.

practiceExercises.prompt: What changes in kauppa (“shop”) → kaupan (“of the shop”)?
practiceExercises.explanation: The double pp becomes one p.

optionFeedback.pp → p: Correct. The double pp becomes one p.
optionFeedback.p → v: “p → v” does not show the required pattern. The double pp becomes one p.
optionFeedback.mp → mm: “mp → mm” does not show the required pattern. The double pp becomes one p.

practiceExercises.prompt: Practice only: matto (“rug”) → ____ (“of the rug”) · use supplied genitive -n; apply tt → t
practiceExercises.explanation: First shorten tt to t, giving mato-, and then read the supplied complete pattern maton.

practiceExercises.prompt: Practice only: kukka (“flower”) → ____ (“of the flower”) · use supplied genitive -n; apply kk → k
practiceExercises.explanation: The supplied target is the genitive meaning “of the flower”, so keep -n fixed. Shorten kk to k: kukka → kuka-, then add -n to make kukan.
